stimulus.text:
Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington, first published in 1800, was a best-selling biography of George Washington. In the fifth edition, published in 1806, Weems added the story of young Washington and the cherry tree:

“I can’t tell a lie, Pa; you know I can’t tell a lie. I did cut it with my hatchet.” — “Run to my arms, you dearest boy,” cried his father in transports, “run to my arms; glad am I, George, that you killed my tree; for you have paid me for it a thousand fold. Such an act of heroism in my son is more worth than a thousand trees, though blossomed with silver, and their fruits of purest gold.”

No evidence supports the story as a real event; Weems said he had heard it from a friend of the Washington family.
stimulus.source_note: Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington (1800; fifth edition 1806). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Mason Locke Weems, The Life of Washington, fifth edition (1806). Public domain.

stem: Weems’s Life of Washington best illustrates which feature of American identity after independence?

options.text: Americans rejected all stories about their leaders as unreliable.
options.misconception: The book was a bestseller, so Americans welcomed such stories rather than rejecting them.

options.text: American writers copied British biographies without changing them.
options.misconception: Weems wrote an American hero’s life for American readers, not a copy of a British book.

options.text: Americans built a national identity through heroic stories.
The founders forbade biographies that praised them.
options.misconception: Background: no founder forbade such biographies, and Weems’s book sold widely.

rationales.C: The book was a bestseller, and its most famous story was invented, yet it shaped how Americans pictured Washington.
rationales.A: A bestseller cannot show Americans rejecting stories about their leaders.
rationales.B: Weems wrote about an American hero for American readers, not a British copy.
rationales.D: Nothing forbade such biographies, and the book’s sales show they were welcomed.
rationales.general:
1. Weems’s Life of Washington was a best-selling biography, first published in 1800.
2. Its most famous story, the cherry tree, was added in 1806 and has no evidence behind it.
3. Background: the books describe such volumes as meant to instill a nationalist spirit in Americans.
4. So the book shows identity built through heroic founder stories, even invented ones.
Remember: a story’s popularity can matter more than its truth for shaping identity.
